scratch_idea: Nucleons are the collective term for the particles found within the atomic nucleus. These include both the positively charged protons and the neutral neutrons.
core_technique: Remember that the mass of a nucleus is almost entirely composed of nucleons, while electrons are excluded.
check_questions: What two particles are collectively called nucleons?
Where are nucleons located in an atom?
Which nucleon has no electrical charge?
common_pitfalls: Including electrons in the nucleon count.
Assuming nucleons only refer to protons.

scratch_idea: The atomic number represents the total number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. It defines the chemical identity of an element.
core_technique: In neutral atoms, the atomic number also equals the number of orbiting electrons.
check_questions: What does the symbol Z represent in nuclear physics?
If an element has 6 protons, what is its atomic number?
Does the atomic number change if a neutron is added to the nucleus?
common_pitfalls: Confusing Z with the total mass of the atom.
Thinking Z includes the number of neutrons.

scratch_idea: The mass number is the total count of protons and neutrons in a nucleus. It indicates the approximate mass of the atom in unified mass units.
core_technique: To find the number of neutrons, subtract Z from A ($N = A - Z$).
check_questions: Define the atomic mass number.
Calculate A for a nucleus with 8 protons and 9 neutrons.
What is the relationship between A, Z, and N?
common_pitfalls: Assuming A is the exact weight in grams.
Forgetting that A is always an integer count of particles.

scratch_idea: The unified atomic mass unit is defined as exactly 1/12th of the mass of a Carbon-12 atom. It is used to express the tiny masses of subatomic particles.
core_technique: Use 931 MeV as the conversion factor when calculating energy released from mass defects.
check_questions: Define 1u in terms of the Carbon-12 atom.
What is the value of 1u in kilograms?
How much energy in MeV corresponds to 1u?
common_pitfalls: Using the mass of a single proton as the definition of 1u.
Confusing the MeV value with the kg value.

scratch_idea: Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. This gives them identical chemical properties but different physical masses.
core_technique: Identify isotopes by looking for the same element symbol but different top-left superscripts.
check_questions: What remains constant among all isotopes of Carbon?
Why do isotopes have different mass numbers?
Give an example of three isotopes of Carbon.
common_pitfalls: Thinking isotopes have different chemical behaviors.
Assuming isotopes of an element must all be radioactive.

scratch_idea: Gravity is an attractive, long-range fundamental force acting between masses. In the context of atomic nuclei, it is the weakest force and is considered negligible.
core_technique: Recognize that while gravity dominates at planetary scales, it plays no significant role in holding a nucleus together.
check_questions: Is the gravitational force attractive or repulsive?
Why is gravity ignored at the atomic level?
What is the range of the gravitational force?
common_pitfalls: Thinking gravity holds the protons and neutrons together.
Assuming the range of gravity is short like nuclear forces.

scratch_idea: The electromagnetic force acts between charged particles. In the nucleus, it causes protons to repel each other, which must be overcome by the strong nuclear force to maintain stability.
core_technique: Understand that electromagnetism is the primary force preventing the nucleus from being stable if only protons were present.
check_questions: How does the electromagnetic force affect two protons in a nucleus?
Who unified electricity and magnetism into one force?
Is the range of electromagnetic force finite or infinite?
common_pitfalls: Forgetting that electromagnetic force acts on protons but not on neutrons.
Confusing the repulsive nature of proton-proton interaction with the nuclear force.

scratch_idea: The strong nuclear force is the most powerful fundamental force, acting only over very short distances ($< 10^{-15}$ m). It binds protons and neutrons together in the nucleus.
core_technique: Note that this force is charge-independent; it attracts p-p, n-n, and p-n equally.
check_questions: What is the range of the strong nuclear force?
Why is this force called 'short-range'?
Does the strong nuclear force depend on the charge of the nucleons?
common_pitfalls: Thinking the strong force acts on electrons.
Assuming the strong force works over macroscopic distances.

scratch_idea: The weak nuclear force is responsible for certain types of radioactive decay, such as beta decay. It is much weaker than the strong force and has an extremely short range.
core_technique: Associate the weak force with the transformation of flavor (e.g., a neutron turning into a proton).
check_questions: Which fundamental force is responsible for beta decay?
How does the range of the weak force compare to the strong force?
What is the relative strength of the weak force compared to the strong force?
common_pitfalls: Confusing the weak nuclear force with the electromagnetic force.
Assuming it is 'weak' enough to be ignored like gravity.

scratch_idea: For every fundamental particle, there exists an antiparticle with the same mass but opposite physical properties like charge and magnetic moment.
core_technique: Identify an antiparticle by a bar over its symbol (e.g., $\bar{p}$) or by a change in charge sign (e.g., $e^+$).
check_questions: What properties do a particle and its antiparticle share?
Name the antiparticle of the electron.
Who predicted the existence of antiparticles in 1928?
common_pitfalls: Thinking antiparticles have negative mass.
Confusing an antiparticle with an isotope.

scratch_idea: Pair production occurs when a high-energy gamma photon interacts with a nucleus and vanishes to create a particle-antiparticle pair (usually electron and positron).
core_technique: Conservation of momentum requires the presence of a nucleus for this process to occur; it cannot happen in a vacuum.
check_questions: What is the minimum energy required for electron-positron pair production?
Why is a nucleus necessary for pair production?
What happens to the excess energy of the photon if its energy is greater than 1.02 MeV?
common_pitfalls: Thinking pair production can occur with visible light.
Forgetting that charge is conserved (one negative, one positive particle produced).

scratch_idea: Annihilation is the reverse of pair production. When a particle and its antiparticle meet, they destroy each other, converting their mass entirely into energy (usually two gamma photons).
core_technique: Note that two photons are emitted in opposite directions to conserve linear momentum.
check_questions: What is produced when an electron and a positron annihilate?
Why are two photons produced instead of just one?
What is the energy of each photon produced in electron-positron annihilation?
common_pitfalls: Thinking the particles just 'disappear' without energy release.
Assuming only electrons and positrons can annihilate.

scratch_idea: Natural radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of radiation (alpha, beta, or gamma) from unstable nuclei, typically those with an atomic number greater than 82.
core_technique: Stability is determined by the neutron-to-proton ratio; once the ratio is off or the nucleus is too large, it becomes radioactive.
check_questions: What is the threshold atomic number for naturally occurring radioactive elements?
Name the three types of radiation emitted during natural radioactivity.
Is radioactivity affected by external physical conditions like temperature?
common_pitfalls: Thinking radioactivity is always caused by external human factors.
Assuming all atoms are radioactive.

scratch_idea: In alpha decay, an unstable nucleus emits an alpha particle (a Helium nucleus). This reduces the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2.
core_technique: Always check that the sum of Z and A on the left side equals the sum of Z and A on the right side.
check_questions: What is the composition of an alpha particle?
How does alpha decay affect the atomic number of the parent element?
If Radium-226 (Z=88) undergoes alpha decay, what is the Z of the daughter nucleus?
common_pitfalls: Forgetting to decrease both A and Z.
Confusing the alpha particle with a lithium nucleus.

scratch_idea: Beta-minus decay occurs when a neutron in the nucleus converts into a proton, an electron (beta particle), and an anti-neutrino.
core_technique: The mass number A remains constant while the atomic number Z increases by 1.
check_questions: What happens to a neutron during beta-minus decay?
What is the purpose of the anti-neutrino in this process?
How does the atomic number change in $\beta^-$ decay?
common_pitfalls: Assuming the mass number A increases.
Forgetting to include the anti-neutrino in the equation.

scratch_idea: Beta-plus decay involves a proton converting into a neutron, a positron, and a neutrino. This happens in nuclei with too many protons.
core_technique: Note that A remains the same, but the atomic number Z decreases by 1.
check_questions: What particle is emitted alongside a neutrino in $\beta^+$ decay?
How does the N/P ratio change during positron emission?
Write the general equation for $\beta^+$ decay.
common_pitfalls: Confusing the positron with a proton.
Forgetting that a neutrino is emitted, not an anti-neutrino.

scratch_idea: Gamma decay is the emission of high-energy electromagnetic radiation from an excited nucleus as it transitions to a lower energy state. No change in A or Z occurs.
core_technique: Look for the asterisk (*) symbol which denotes an excited state of the nucleus.
check_questions: Does gamma decay change the identity of the element?
What is the nature of gamma radiation?
Why does a nucleus undergo gamma decay?
common_pitfalls: Thinking gamma rays have charge.
Expecting a change in the mass number.

scratch_idea: Alpha particles emitted from a specific radionuclide all possess fixed, distinct kinetic energy values, appearing as sharp lines on an energy spectrum.
core_technique: Contrast this with beta decay; alpha decay is a two-body problem (daughter nucleus + alpha), hence fixed energies.
check_questions: Describe the energy spectrum of alpha particles.
What does 'discrete energy' mean in the context of decay?
Why do alpha particles have fixed energies?
common_pitfalls: Confusing the discrete spectrum of alpha with the continuous spectrum of beta.
Assuming the energy of alpha particles from different sources is the same.

scratch_idea: Beta particles are emitted with a range of energies from zero to a maximum because the decay energy is shared between the beta particle and the (anti)neutrino.
core_technique: The three-body nature of beta decay (daughter + beta + neutrino) allows for variable energy distribution.
check_questions: Why is the beta energy spectrum continuous rather than discrete?
Who proposed the neutrino to explain this energy sharing?
What happens to the total energy in a beta decay event?
common_pitfalls: Assuming all beta particles from the same source have the same speed.
Thinking the missing energy violates conservation of energy laws.

scratch_idea: Hadrons are complex particles made of quarks that interact via the strong nuclear force. They are divided into baryons and mesons.
core_technique: If a particle experiences the strong force, it must be a hadron.
check_questions: What defines a hadron?
Give two examples of hadrons.
Into what two categories are hadrons divided?
common_pitfalls: Including electrons in the hadron family.
Assuming all hadrons are stable.

scratch_idea: Leptons are truly fundamental particles that do not experience the strong nuclear force. Examples include electrons, muons, and neutrinos.
core_technique: Leptons are characterized by their lack of internal quark structure.
check_questions: List three particles belonging to the lepton family.
Do leptons interact via the strong nuclear force?
Are leptons considered composite or fundamental particles?
common_pitfalls: Confusing leptons with mesons.
Thinking protons are leptons because they are small.

scratch_idea: Baryons are a type of hadron made of exactly three quarks. Protons and neutrons are the most common baryons.
core_technique: Check for an odd number of quarks (specifically 3) to identify a baryon.
check_questions: How many quarks make up a baryon?
Is a proton a baryon or a meson?
What is the baryon number of a proton?
common_pitfalls: Confusing the term baryon with nucleon (though they overlap).
Thinking mesons are baryons.

scratch_idea: Mesons are hadrons composed of one quark and one anti-quark. They are typically short-lived and act as mediators of forces between nucleons.
core_technique: Remember the quark-antiquark pair structure ($q\bar{q}$).
check_questions: What is the quark composition of a meson?
Name one example of a meson.
Are mesons considered fermions or bosons?
common_pitfalls: Thinking mesons are made of three quarks.
Confusing mesons with muons (which are leptons).

scratch_idea: There are six types of quarks, known as flavors: up (u), down (d), strange (s), charm (c), bottom (b), and top (t).
core_technique: Memorize the charges: Up-type (u, c, t) are +2/3, and Down-type (d, s, b) are -1/3.
check_questions: How many quark flavors exist?
What is the electric charge of a 'down' quark?
Which quark has the highest mass?
common_pitfalls: Thinking quarks have integer charges.
Confusing flavor with color charge.

scratch_idea: A proton consists of two up quarks and one down quark (uud). The fractional charges add up to a net charge of +1.
core_technique: Use the uud formula to derive why the proton has a +1 charge.
check_questions: What is the quark content of a proton?
Show how the fractional charges of quarks result in a charge of +1 for the proton.
How many 'down' quarks are in a proton?
common_pitfalls: Mixing up the composition with that of the neutron (udd).
Forgetting that quarks are held together by gluons.

scratch_idea: A neutron is composed of one up quark and two down quarks (udd). These fractional charges cancel out to a net charge of zero.
core_technique: Use the udd formula to prove the neutron's neutrality.
check_questions: Identify the three quarks that form a neutron.
Why is a neutron electrically neutral in terms of quarks?
Which quark is more prevalent in a neutron, up or down?
common_pitfalls: Confusing 'udd' with 'uud'.
Thinking the neutron has no internal charge structure.

scratch_idea: Quarks possess a property called 'color charge' (red, green, blue). The strong force between quarks is called the color force, and all observed hadrons must be 'colorless' (white).
core_technique: Baryons contain one red, one green, and one blue quark, while mesons contain a color and its anti-color.
check_questions: What are the three types of color charges?
What does 'colorless' mean in the context of a baryon?
Which theory describes the interaction of color charges?
common_pitfalls: Thinking quarks are actually colored like light.
Confusing color charge with electric charge.

scratch_idea: At the most fundamental level, beta-minus decay is the conversion of a 'down' quark into an 'up' quark, releasing an electron and an anti-neutrino.
core_technique: Focus on the change from udd (neutron) to uud (proton).
check_questions: Which quark changes its flavor during beta-minus decay?
Write the fundamental quark equation for $\beta^-$ decay.
How does the quark composition change when a neutron becomes a proton?
common_pitfalls: Thinking the whole nucleon disappears.
Assuming the 'up' quark turns into a 'down' quark in $\beta^-$ decay.

scratch_idea: The Higgs boson is a fundamental particle that interacts with the Higgs field. This interaction is what gives other fundamental particles their mass.
core_technique: Think of the Higgs field as a 'syrup' that permeates space; particles that 'drag' more in it become heavier.
check_questions: What is the primary role of the Higgs Boson in particle physics?
In which year was the Higgs Boson discovered at CERN?
Why do photons have no rest mass according to Higgs theory?
common_pitfalls: Thinking the Higgs Boson 'is' mass.
Assuming it gives mass to composite objects like humans directly (most of our mass comes from binding energy).

scratch_idea: Forces are transmitted between particles by the exchange of gauge bosons. For example, photons carry the electromagnetic force and gluons carry the strong force.
core_technique: Match the boson to the force: Photon (EM), Gluon (Strong), W/Z (Weak), Graviton (Gravity).
check_questions: What particle mediates the electromagnetic interaction?
Name the force carrier for the strong nuclear force.
Which particles are responsible for the weak nuclear force?
common_pitfalls: Confusing the mediator with the particle being acted upon.
Thinking the graviton has been experimentally confirmed like the photon.

topic_name: Conservation of Nucleon and Charge Number
scratch_idea: In all nuclear processes, the total number of nucleons (A) and the total electric charge (Z) must remain constant from the beginning to the end of the reaction.
core_technique: Use this law to find 'missing' particles in nuclear equations by balancing the top and bottom numbers.
check_questions: State the law of conservation of nucleon number.
If a nucleus with Z=90 decays and an alpha particle (Z=2) is released, what is the Z of the remaining nucleus?
Does the total mass-energy always remain conserved in nuclear reactions?
common_pitfalls: Forgetting to include the charge of emitted electrons or positrons in the Z balance.
Thinking mass is conserved separately from energy.

scratch_idea: The observable universe is composed almost entirely of matter. The reason why there isn't an equal amount of anti-matter (which would lead to total annihilation) is an unsolved mystery in physics.
core_technique: Understand that the imbalance likely stems from a violation of baryon number conservation in the early universe.
check_questions: What percentage of the observable universe is matter vs anti-matter?
What is the 'mystery' regarding matter and anti-matter in the Big Bang theory?
Why doesn't the universe contain equal parts of hydrogen and anti-hydrogen?
common_pitfalls: Assuming anti-matter doesn't exist at all.
Confusing dark matter with anti-matter.

scratch_idea: Most of the visible matter in the universe (stars, nebulae) exists in the plasma state—a gas of ions and free electrons. 95% of ordinary matter is estimated to be plasma.
core_technique: Distinguish between the total universe (mostly dark energy/matter) and the 'observable' ordinary matter (mostly plasma).
check_questions: What is the most common state of ordinary matter in the universe?
Why is most matter in stars in the plasma state?
What percentage of ordinary matter is estimated to be plasma?
common_pitfalls: Thinking solids are the most common state of matter in the universe.
Forgetting that the 95% figure refers to the 5% of 'ordinary' matter.

scratch_idea: The Standard Model is the theoretical framework that organizes all known fundamental particles (quarks, leptons, and bosons) and their interactions, excluding gravity.
core_technique: Identify the Standard Model as a 'Periodic Table' for subatomic particles.
check_questions: Which three categories of particles form the Standard Model?
What major force is not currently explained by the Standard Model?
What role does the Higgs boson play in the Standard Model?
common_pitfalls: Thinking the Standard Model is a complete 'Theory of Everything'.
Assuming it includes a description of Dark Matter.
